text: APA in-text citation should use author-date form and clearly distinguish narrative citation from parenthetical citation within the sentence context.
Publication years should be placed in parentheses when required by APA citation syntax and kept consistent across repeated source mentions.
Every empirical or quantitative claim should be attached to a specific and verifiable source within the same paragraph.
GB/T numbered references should correspond to complete bibliography entries with author title year and source type.
Citation feedback should evaluate whether a reader can trace a claim to a concrete source.
A single broad citation at the end of a paragraph should not hide multiple unsupported literature claims.
An abstract should state problem objective method evaluation result and contribution in a coherent sequence.
Abstract elements are weak when solution and implementation details appear before the research problem and objective.
An introduction should move from background to problem to research gap before presenting the contribution.
The contribution statement should answer the identified research gap rather than only list product features.
IMRAD writing should keep method procedure separate from results and discussion interpretation in every manuscript section.
Result claims should appear in the results section rather than inside the method description where readers expect evidence.
The results section should report measured experimental outcomes instead of repeating interface design details or implementation rationale.
Evaluation results should include metrics such as node existence rate threshold pass rate and feedback completion.
A conclusion should synthesize established findings and avoid introducing new unsupported claims beyond the reported evidence.
Limitations should state what the study cannot prove and define boundaries for interpretation and later generalization.
A background paragraph should establish the educational or research context before technical implementation details or system architecture choices.
Paragraphs should sequence context problem and technical response so readers understand why the design is needed.
A method paragraph should describe data procedure configuration and metrics so another researcher can reproduce the study.
A result paragraph should report measured findings with numbers comparisons and concise interpretation tied to the stated evaluation question.
A paragraph should use a clear topic sentence and keep sentence roles aligned with its main function.
A discussion paragraph should interpret findings rather than merely repeat numerical results without adding unsupported methodological claims.
Discussion should explain mechanisms implications and constraints without inventing new experimental data or overstating causal conclusions.
A limitation paragraph should clearly state evidence boundaries and future work instead of promotional claims.
Citation format quality should be judged by traceability, style consistency, source completeness, and the proximity between claims and supporting references.
Section structure quality should be judged by functional boundaries, expected rhetorical order, evidence placement, and consistency with IMRAD conventions.
Paragraph function quality should be judged by topic sentence clarity, sentence-role alignment, and whether one paragraph performs one dominant role.
Paragraph completeness quality should be judged by cohesion, sufficient evidence, logical sequencing, and closure that supports the paragraph purpose.
Research-report organization should be evaluated by whether each section answers its expected question without borrowing functions from neighboring sections.
APA narrative citations should place the author in the sentence grammar and the year in parentheses near the cited claim.
APA parenthetical citations should place author and year together in parentheses after the paraphrased claim or sentence segment.
When paraphrasing a source, the writer must still cite the original author using the appropriate in-text citation format.
Direct quotations should use quotation marks, include an in-text citation, and provide a page, paragraph, or locator when available.
Secondary citations should identify the original work in the prose and cite the consulted source with an as-cited-in formulation.
APA journal article references should include authors, year, article title, journal title, volume, issue, page range, and DOI when available.
APA book references should include authors, publication year, italicized title, edition when relevant, publisher, and DOI or URL if available.
Conference paper references should identify the authors, year, paper title, conference name, location or publisher, page range, and persistent link.
Web resource references should provide author, date, page title, website name, URL, and retrieval date when content is designed to change.
GB/T 7714 sequential coding should assign bracketed numbers by citation order and match each number to one bibliography entry.
Reference lists should use one citation style consistently, sort entries according to that style, and disambiguate same-author same-year works with suffixes.
Smith (2020) argues that feedback timing influences revision quality, which demonstrates a narrative APA citation embedded in the sentence.
Feedback timing can influence revision quality when students receive comments before drafting is complete (Smith, 2020).
The sentence reports a direct phrase as quoted language and places the author, year, and page number immediately after it.
A journal reference lists the author group, year, article title, journal title, volume, issue, pages, and DOI in one entry.
In GB/T sequential style, the first cited source appears as bracketed number one and the bibliography begins with that same entry.
A secondary citation names the original theory in prose while the parenthetical citation identifies the source that the writer actually read.
The paragraph ends with one broad citation even though it contains separate claims about adoption rate, learning effect, and model accuracy.
The manuscript uses an in-text citation for a study, but the reference list contains no matching bibliography entry.
The in-text citation follows APA author-date style while the bibliography uses numbered GB/T entries, creating a mixed citation system.
A sentence copies distinctive wording from a source but presents it without quotation marks, locator information, or direct quotation formatting.
The text cites a classic author through another paper but does not reveal that the original source was not consulted.
Attach citations to individual empirical claims, and split the paragraph when different evidence streams support different statements.
Add a complete reference entry for every in-text citation or remove the citation when the source cannot be verified.
Choose one citation style for the manuscript and revise both in-text citations and bibliography entries to match it.
Convert copied wording into a marked direct quotation, add a locator, or paraphrase it fully with a normal citation.
Use an as-cited-in phrase for secondary citation and list only the consulted source in the reference list unless required otherwise.
Normalize the reference list by sorting entries, completing missing fields, and resolving same-author same-year ambiguity before final submission.
IMRAD sections should maintain functional boundaries so methods explain procedure, results present findings, and discussion interprets those findings.
An abstract should concisely state the research problem, objective, method, key result, and conclusion in a reader-oriented sequence.
An introduction should establish background, identify a research gap, explain why it matters, and then state the study contribution.
A methods section should provide enough data, procedure, implementation configuration, and evaluation metric detail for another researcher to reproduce the work.
A results section should present measured outcomes, tables, and comparisons without shifting into broad interpretation or literature explanation.
A discussion section should explain findings, compare them with prior literature, identify mechanisms, and acknowledge limitations or boundary conditions.
A conclusion should synthesize verified findings, answer the research objective, and avoid introducing new claims not supported by earlier sections.
A limitation statement should define evidence boundaries, sample constraints, measurement constraints, and conditions under which findings should not be generalized.
The abstract first identifies the feedback problem, then names the retrieval method, reports evaluation gains, and closes with the study contribution.
The introduction moves from writing-feedback research to an unresolved traceability gap before presenting the proposed graph-based contribution.
The methods section specifies the query set, norm-node corpus, retrieval settings, threshold values, and scoring procedure for replication.
The results section reports that one method retrieved more valid reference nodes than another under the same threshold setting.
The discussion explains why graph expansion improved traceability and relates the pattern to earlier work on structured feedback.
The conclusion summarizes verified retrieval gains and states that broader classroom effectiveness remains outside the current evidence boundary.
The methods section reports final accuracy and pass-rate improvements before explaining the dataset, settings, or evaluation procedure.
The abstract spends most sentences on implementation details while omitting the research problem, principal result, and conclusion.
The conclusion claims a teaching-effectiveness improvement that was never tested in the reported experiment or supported by earlier results.
The discussion repeats metric values from the results section but never explains mechanisms, implications, contradictions, or limitations.
The introduction lists tool features immediately after background without defining a research gap or explaining the scholarly contribution.
Move measured outcomes from the methods section into results, and keep methods focused on data, procedure, configuration, and metrics.
Rewrite the abstract around problem, objective, method, result, and conclusion before adding only essential implementation detail.
Add a research gap sentence and connect the contribution statement directly to that gap instead of listing functions.
Separate result reporting from discussion by moving numbers to results and reserving discussion for explanation and literature connection.
Revise the conclusion so it only synthesizes tested findings, states implications cautiously, and avoids new unverified claims.
Add a limitations sentence that names sample scope, measurement constraints, and evidence boundaries before proposing future work.
A paragraph should open with a topic sentence that identifies its main claim, function, or contribution to the section.
A background paragraph should define the research context and motivation before moving into technical design, parameters, or implementation detail.
A method paragraph should specify data, procedure, configuration, instruments, and metrics rather than only naming the implemented system.
A result paragraph should include concrete values, comparisons, and observed patterns while keeping interpretation concise and evidence-bound.
A discussion paragraph should explain the meaning of findings, possible mechanisms, relation to literature, and implications for the research question.
A limitation paragraph should name the evidence boundary, describe why it matters, and avoid presenting limitations as promotional strengths.
Paragraph cohesion should be maintained through logical sentence order, explicit transitions, repeated key terms, and clear referents.
Paragraph completeness requires enough context, evidence, explanation, and closure for the reader to understand the local claim.
One paragraph should perform one dominant rhetorical function and should not mix unrelated background, method, result, and discussion tasks.
Supporting sentences should elaborate, qualify, or evidence the topic sentence instead of adding side claims that distract from the paragraph purpose.
A background paragraph begins by naming the writing-feedback problem and then explains why traceable norm references matter for revision.
A method paragraph lists the query set, norm-node corpus, retrieval method, threshold setting, and evaluation metrics used in the experiment.
A result paragraph states that one method retrieved fifteen valid references while another retrieved eleven under the same evaluation condition.
A discussion paragraph explains that graph expansion may improve traceability because it links errors to norms and revision suggestions.
A limitation paragraph states that the query set is synthetic and therefore cannot prove classroom learning effects.
A cohesive paragraph repeats the key term traceability, uses this result to connect sentences, and closes by returning to the topic claim.
The paragraph begins with isolated implementation detail and never states the central claim that the following sentences are meant to support.
A background paragraph starts with vector dimensions, threshold settings, and database choices before explaining the research context.
A method paragraph names an experiment but omits the data source, procedure, configuration, instruments, and evaluation metrics.
A result paragraph claims improvement but gives no numerical value, comparison baseline, threshold condition, or observed pattern.
A discussion paragraph repeats the reported scores but does not explain significance, mechanism, literature connection, or limitation.
One paragraph mixes literature background, system configuration, result numbers, and future teaching claims without a controlling function.
Add a topic sentence that names the paragraph function and revise later sentences so they support that single claim.
Expand the paragraph with missing data, procedure, metric, numerical result, or comparison information required by its function.
Split sentences with different rhetorical functions into separate paragraphs, then order each paragraph around one explicit purpose.
